passage: Women have historically been paid less. But in the US in the 1980s, they began to catch up — fast. During that decade, the gender pay gap closed by about one percentage point a year. Had that trend continued, the gender wage gap would have been closed by 2017. But the trend didn’t continue, and the gap remains yawning. counterintuitively, to the introduction of state and federal family leave policies. Those monitoring the process towards salary equity at work have long watched as progress slowed in many countries around the world. In fact, that progress began to reverse during the pandemic (大流行病). The gender pay gap is one of the most outstanding examples of that lack of parity (平等), and still exists just about everywhere. The motherhood penalty has become a shorthand for describing why: In many places, especially rich countries, women earn the same as men until they reach their childbearing years. Women who have children begin to see their salaries slip behind their male counterparts. Part of this is because women take on more of the unpaid labor at home, which can eat into time available for work and energy for career advancement. questions.q: What happened with the introduction of state and federal family leave policies?
options: The process towards salary equity at work began to reverse.
The rate of gender wage convergence started to fall noticeably.
The trend of women returning to work after childbirth started.

questions.q: What partly accounts for the slip in women’s salaries?
options: The insufficient motivation women generally have for career advancement.
The opportunities numerous women give up for pay raise and promotion.
The huge amounts of time and energy women spend taking care of the family.
The lack of policy support from government and business corporations.

questions.q: What does the new study say about wage parity？
options: It would have stalled if those controllable problems had not been addressed.

questions.q: What prevents women from achieving parity with men in the final analysis?
options: Ignoring biases against women in the workplace.
Failing to mandate breaks for childbirth and care.
Giving birth to children and taking care of them.
Lacking resources to address biological problems.
